stem: 'Primary activities' are economic activities that __________.
options: Involve extracting and producing goods directly from nature (from the Earth's natural resources)
Only involve manufacturing goods in factories
Only involve research and information technology
solution: PRIMARY ACTIVITIES are economic activities that involve EXTRACTING and PRODUCING goods DIRECTLY from NATURE — i.e., using the Earth's NATURAL RESOURCES. They include activities like hunting and gathering, pastoralism (animal rearing), agriculture (farming), fishing, forestry (lumbering), and mining/quarrying. Primary activities are 'primary' because they are the first, most basic stage of economic production, obtaining raw materials from the natural environment (which secondary activities then process). So primary activities involve extracting goods directly from nature. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a primary activity?
options: Agriculture, hunting and gathering, fishing, forestry (lumbering), pastoralism, and mining
solution: PRIMARY ACTIVITIES include: AGRICULTURE (crop farming); HUNTING and GATHERING; FISHING; FORESTRY/LUMBERING (obtaining wood); PASTORALISM (rearing animals — herding); and MINING and quarrying (extracting minerals). All of these obtain raw materials or food DIRECTLY from NATURE. (Manufacturing cars is a secondary activity; banking, insurance, and software are tertiary/quaternary — service/knowledge — activities.) So agriculture, hunting-gathering, fishing, forestry, pastoralism, and mining are primary activities. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The most primitive/oldest form of primary activity, in which people depend on nature for food by collecting wild plants and hunting animals, is __________.
solution: HUNTING and GATHERING (food gathering/collecting) is the most PRIMITIVE and OLDEST form of primary activity. In it, people depend directly on NATURE for FOOD by COLLECTING wild plants, fruits, roots, and nuts (gathering) and HUNTING wild animals for meat. It requires low technology and small populations, and it was the way of life of early humans; today only a few isolated communities (in dense forests, deserts, and remote regions) still practise it. So the oldest primary activity is hunting and gathering. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Pastoralism' (animal rearing/herding) is of two main types. These are __________.
options: Nomadic herding (pastoral nomadism) and commercial livestock rearing (commercial pastoralism/ranching)
solution: PASTORALISM (the rearing of animals/herding) is of two main types: (1) NOMADIC HERDING (pastoral nomadism) — a subsistence activity in which herders MOVE with their animals (cattle, sheep, goats, camels, yaks, reindeer) from place to place in search of pasture and water, common in harsh, dry, or cold regions; and (2) COMMERCIAL LIVESTOCK REARING (commercial pastoralism/RANCHING) — a more organised, capital-intensive activity in which animals are reared on large fenced areas (ranches) for the MARKET (meat, wool, hides), practised in regions like the USA, Argentina, Australia, and New Zealand. So the two types are nomadic herding and commercial livestock rearing. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Subsistence agriculture' refers to farming in which __________.
options: Farmers grow crops mainly to feed themselves and their families (for their own consumption), with little or no surplus for sale
Crops are grown only for factories
No crops are grown at all
solution: SUBSISTENCE AGRICULTURE refers to farming in which farmers grow crops (and rear animals) MAINLY to FEED THEMSELVES and their FAMILIES — for their OWN CONSUMPTION — with LITTLE or NO SURPLUS left over for sale in the market. It is typically small-scale, uses simple tools and family labour, and is common in developing countries. (It contrasts with commercial agriculture, which produces crops for sale/profit.) So subsistence agriculture is farming for the farmer's own consumption. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Shifting cultivation' (slash-and-burn agriculture) is a form of subsistence farming in which __________.
options: A patch of forest is cleared (by cutting and burning), cultivated for a few years, then abandoned for a new patch when the soil loses fertility
The same field is used forever with heavy machinery
Crops are grown only in cities
solution: SHIFTING CULTIVATION (slash-and-burn agriculture) is a form of PRIMITIVE SUBSISTENCE farming in which a PATCH of FOREST is CLEARED (by CUTTING down and BURNING the vegetation — 'slash and burn'), then CULTIVATED for a FEW YEARS. When the SOIL loses its FERTILITY, the patch is ABANDONED and the farmers move on to CLEAR a NEW patch, allowing the old one to regenerate. It is practised in tropical regions (known by names like jhum in India, milpa, ladang, etc.). It supports small populations but can cause deforestation if cycles shorten. So shifting cultivation clears, cultivates, and abandons forest patches in rotation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Commercial agriculture' is characterised by __________.
options: Growing crops and rearing animals mainly for sale in the market (for profit), often on a large scale with modern methods
Growing food only for the farmer's family
solution: COMMERCIAL AGRICULTURE is characterised by growing CROPS and rearing ANIMALS mainly for SALE in the MARKET (for PROFIT), rather than for the farmer's own consumption. It is typically practised on a LARGER SCALE, with MODERN METHODS (machinery, high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, irrigation) and often specialisation in particular crops or products. Types include commercial grain farming, mixed farming, plantation agriculture, and commercial livestock rearing. So commercial agriculture produces mainly for the market/profit. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Plantation agriculture' is a type of commercial farming characterised by __________.
options: Large estates growing a single cash crop (like tea, coffee, rubber, or sugarcane) for export, using much labour and capital
Growing many different food crops for local families
solution: PLANTATION AGRICULTURE is a type of COMMERCIAL farming characterised by LARGE ESTATES (plantations) that grow a SINGLE CASH CROP (MONOCULTURE) — such as TEA, COFFEE, RUBBER, SUGARCANE, cotton, bananas, or oil palm — primarily for EXPORT. It uses a large amount of LABOUR and CAPITAL, is often located in tropical/subtropical regions, and was historically associated with colonial economies. So plantation agriculture grows a single cash crop on large estates for export. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Mining' is a primary activity that involves __________.
options: Extracting minerals and other valuable materials from the Earth (from beneath or on the surface)
solution: MINING is a primary activity that involves EXTRACTING MINERALS and other valuable materials (metals, coal, oil and gas, precious stones, etc.) from the EARTH — from BENEATH the surface (underground/shaft mining) or from the SURFACE (open-cast/surface mining). Mining provides the raw materials (like iron ore, coal, bauxite) that fuel industries and modern economies. It is a primary activity because it directly extracts resources from nature. So mining is the extraction of minerals from the Earth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The two main methods of mining are __________.
solution: The two main METHODS of MINING are: (1) SURFACE (OPEN-CAST/open-pit) MINING — where minerals lying NEAR the SURFACE are extracted by removing the overlying soil and rock (cheaper, safer, and used when deposits are shallow); and (2) UNDERGROUND (SHAFT) MINING — where DEEP deposits are reached by sinking vertical SHAFTS and horizontal galleries into the Earth (more expensive, dangerous, and used for deep-lying minerals). The method chosen depends on the depth and nature of the mineral deposit. So the two main mining methods are surface (open-cast) and underground (shaft) mining. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Primary activities are more important (as a share of employment) in developing countries than in developed ones. Reason (R): Developing economies rely heavily on agriculture and other primary activities, while developed economies have shifted toward industry and services. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that PRIMARY ACTIVITIES are MORE IMPORTANT (as a share of employment) in DEVELOPING countries than in developed ones. And the reason is (R) that DEVELOPING economies RELY HEAVILY on AGRICULTURE and other primary activities (a large share of their workforce is engaged in farming, etc.), WHILE DEVELOPED economies have SHIFTED toward INDUSTRY (secondary) and especially SERVICES (tertiary), with only a small fraction of workers in primary activities. This difference in the stage of economic development directly explains the greater weight of primary activities in developing countries (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: 'Intensive subsistence agriculture' (common in densely populated parts of monsoon Asia) is characterised by __________.
options: Cultivation of small plots intensively (with much labour) to get maximum output — often rice-dominated, to feed dense populations
solution: INTENSIVE SUBSISTENCE AGRICULTURE (common in the densely populated parts of MONSOON ASIA — including India, China, and Southeast Asia) is characterised by cultivating SMALL PLOTS of land very INTENSIVELY, using a LARGE amount of LABOUR (and manures, and multiple cropping) to obtain the MAXIMUM OUTPUT per unit of land. It is often dominated by RICE (in wetter areas) and other food grains, and is aimed at FEEDING the DENSE POPULATIONS of these regions. Land is scarce relative to people, so it is farmed intensively. So intensive subsistence agriculture farms small plots intensively for maximum food output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Market gardening' and 'horticulture' are types of commercial farming that specialise in __________.
options: Growing high-value vegetables, fruits, and flowers for urban markets
Growing only staple grains for subsistence
solution: MARKET GARDENING and HORTICULTURE are types of intensive COMMERCIAL farming that SPECIALISE in growing HIGH-VALUE VEGETABLES, FRUITS, and FLOWERS for sale — especially to nearby URBAN MARKETS (cities with wealthy consumers who demand fresh produce). These are labour- and capital-intensive activities located near cities or with good transport links, aimed at profit. (A related form, 'truck farming', grows vegetables for distant markets.) So market gardening/horticulture grows high-value vegetables, fruits, and flowers for urban markets. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Fishing' as a primary activity is important because __________.
options: It provides food (a major source of protein), employment, and raw materials, and rich fishing grounds are found especially in cool waters over continental shelves
It is not an economic activity
solution: FISHING is an important primary activity because it provides FOOD (fish are a major source of PROTEIN for much of the world's population), EMPLOYMENT (for millions of people), and RAW MATERIALS (for products like fish oil, fish meal, and fertiliser). The RICHEST FISHING GROUNDS are found especially in COOL WATERS over the CONTINENTAL SHELVES (shallow, nutrient-rich seas where cold and warm currents meet, supporting abundant plankton and fish) — such as the North Sea, the Grand Banks, and the seas off Japan and Peru. So fishing provides food, jobs, and raw materials, especially from cool continental-shelf waters. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Nomadic herding' (pastoral nomadism) is generally practised in __________.
options: Harsh regions unsuitable for crop farming — such as semi-arid, arid, and cold areas (e.g., the Sahara fringes, Central Asia, and the Arctic tundra)
solution: NOMADIC HERDING (pastoral nomadism) is generally practised in HARSH REGIONS that are UNSUITABLE for CROP FARMING — such as SEMI-ARID and ARID areas (the fringes of the Sahara and the deserts of Arabia and Central Asia), and COLD areas (the ARCTIC TUNDRA of northern Eurasia). In these environments where cultivation is difficult, people rear hardy animals (camels, sheep, goats, cattle, yaks, reindeer) and MOVE with them in search of pasture and water. So nomadic herding is practised in harsh semi-arid, arid, and cold regions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Mixed farming' is a type of commercial agriculture in which __________.
options: Both crops are grown and animals are reared on the same farm (combining crop cultivation and livestock)
Only animals are kept with no crops
solution: MIXED FARMING is a type of COMMERCIAL agriculture in which BOTH CROPS are GROWN and ANIMALS (livestock) are REARED on the SAME FARM. Farmers combine crop cultivation (grains, fodder) with keeping animals (cattle, pigs, poultry), so the two support each other (e.g., crops and fodder feed the animals, and animal manure fertilises the crops), spreading risk and using resources efficiently. It is common in the developed regions of Europe, North America, and elsewhere. So mixed farming combines crop cultivation and livestock rearing on the same farm. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Dairy farming' is a form of commercial livestock/agriculture that specialises in __________.
options: Rearing milch animals (cattle) for milk and dairy products, often located near urban markets
solution: DAIRY FARMING is a form of intensive COMMERCIAL livestock farming that SPECIALISES in REARING MILCH ANIMALS (dairy CATTLE, and sometimes buffaloes) for MILK and dairy PRODUCTS (butter, cheese, etc.). Because milk is perishable, dairy farms are often located NEAR URBAN MARKETS (or with good refrigerated transport). It is highly labour- and capital-intensive (requiring care, feeding, and modern facilities), and is well developed in regions like North-western Europe, North America, New Zealand, and Australia. So dairy farming rears cattle for milk and dairy products, often near markets. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Commercial grain farming' (extensive) is characterised by __________.
options: Growing grains (mainly wheat) on very large farms with machinery for the market, in temperate grassland regions (like the Prairies, Steppes, Pampas)
Growing rice on tiny plots by hand
solution: COMMERCIAL GRAIN FARMING (extensive commercial farming) is characterised by growing GRAINS — mainly WHEAT (and maize, barley) — on VERY LARGE FARMS with extensive use of MACHINERY (tractors, harvesters), for the MARKET/export. It is practised in the TEMPERATE GRASSLAND regions of the world — such as the PRAIRIES of North America, the STEPPES of Eurasia, the PAMPAS of Argentina, and the Downs of Australia — which have large, flat expanses, fertile soils, and low population density, making large-scale mechanised grain farming possible. So commercial grain farming grows wheat on large mechanised farms in temperate grasslands. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Shifting cultivation can lead to environmental problems when practised intensively. Reason (R): If the same land is reused too quickly (short fallow periods) due to population pressure, the soil and forest cannot recover, causing degradation and deforestation. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that SHIFTING CULTIVATION can lead to ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS when practised intensively. And the reason is (R) that if the SAME LAND is REUSED TOO QUICKLY (with SHORT FALLOW/rest PERIODS) — due to rising POPULATION PRESSURE — the SOIL and FOREST cannot fully RECOVER between cultivations, leading to SOIL DEGRADATION (loss of fertility, erosion) and DEFORESTATION. Traditionally, long fallow periods allowed regeneration; when these are shortened, the sustainable balance breaks down. This inability to recover directly causes the environmental harm (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Forestry (lumbering) as a primary activity involves __________.
options: The commercial harvesting of timber and wood products from forests
solution: FORESTRY (LUMBERING) as a primary activity involves the COMMERCIAL HARVESTING of TIMBER (wood) and other WOOD PRODUCTS from FORESTS — cutting and gathering trees for use as lumber, pulp (for paper), and fuel. Major commercial lumbering occurs in the vast coniferous (softwood) forests of the temperate regions (e.g., Canada, the USA, Russia, and Scandinavia) and in tropical hardwood forests. Being the extraction of a natural resource (wood) from the environment, forestry is a primary activity. So forestry/lumbering is the harvesting of timber from forests. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Extensive' versus 'intensive' agriculture differ in that __________.
options: Extensive farming uses large areas of land with less labour/inputs per unit area; intensive farming uses small areas with much labour/inputs per unit area
Extensive means small plots; intensive means large farms
solution: EXTENSIVE and INTENSIVE agriculture differ in the use of land relative to labour and inputs. EXTENSIVE farming uses LARGE AREAS of LAND with RELATIVELY LITTLE LABOUR and inputs per unit area — output per hectare is low, but total output is large due to the vast area (e.g., commercial grain farming on the Prairies, with machines on huge farms). INTENSIVE farming uses SMALL AREAS of land with a LARGE amount of LABOUR and inputs (fertiliser, irrigation) per unit area — achieving HIGH output per hectare (e.g., intensive subsistence rice farming in monsoon Asia). The distinction reflects the land-labour ratio and how heavily land is worked. So extensive = large land/low inputs per area; intensive = small land/high inputs per area. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The type of agriculture practised in a region depends on factors such as __________.
options: Physical factors (climate, soil, relief, water) and human factors (population, technology, markets, capital, government policy)
Only the colour of the sky
Only the day of the week
solution: The TYPE of AGRICULTURE practised in a region DEPENDS on a combination of factors: PHYSICAL factors — CLIMATE (temperature, rainfall), SOIL type and fertility, RELIEF (flat vs hilly land), and WATER availability (which determine what can be grown and how); and HUMAN factors — POPULATION density (land-labour ratio), TECHNOLOGY (machinery, seeds, irrigation), MARKETS (demand and access), CAPITAL (investment), and GOVERNMENT POLICY. The interplay of these natural and human factors shapes whether farming is subsistence or commercial, intensive or extensive, and which crops are grown. So agricultural type depends on physical and human factors. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Primary activities are the foundation of the economy because __________.
options: They provide the food and raw materials on which secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (service) activities depend
solution: PRIMARY ACTIVITIES are the FOUNDATION of the economy because they PROVIDE the FOOD (from agriculture, fishing, herding) and the RAW MATERIALS (minerals from mining, wood from forestry, fibres and produce from farming) on which the SECONDARY (manufacturing — which processes raw materials into goods) and TERTIARY (service) activities DEPEND. Without primary activities supplying these basic inputs, industry and services could not function. Thus primary production underpins the whole economic structure. So primary activities are foundational because they supply food and raw materials for other sectors. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, the various primary activities reflect __________.
options: Different ways in which humans use the natural environment and its resources to obtain food and materials, ranging from primitive/subsistence to modern/commercial forms
solution: In summary, the various PRIMARY ACTIVITIES REFLECT the DIFFERENT WAYS in which HUMANS USE the NATURAL ENVIRONMENT and its RESOURCES to obtain FOOD and MATERIALS. They RANGE from PRIMITIVE/SUBSISTENCE forms (hunting and gathering, nomadic herding, shifting and intensive subsistence cultivation), where people depend closely on nature with simple technology, to MODERN/COMMERCIAL forms (commercial grain and mixed farming, plantations, ranching, dairying, mechanised fishing and mining), where nature's resources are exploited on a large scale with advanced technology for the market. This spectrum illustrates the evolving human–environment relationship in economic life. So primary activities reflect the varied ways humans use nature's resources, from subsistence to commercial. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Primary Activities' is that:
options: Primary activities are unimportant to the economy

PRIMARY ACTIVITIES are the economic activities that extract and produce goods DIRECTLY from NATURE (the Earth's resources) — including hunting and gathering (the oldest), pastoralism (nomadic herding and commercial ranching), agriculture (ranging from primitive subsistence/shifting cultivation and intensive subsistence farming to commercial farming like grain, plantation, and market gardening), fishing, forestry, and mining; they form the FIRST/BASIC stage of economic production, supplying food and raw materials, and are MORE IMPORTANT (in employment) in DEVELOPING countries than developed ones (whose economies have shifted to industry and services); the type and methods of primary activities vary with the natural environment, technology, and level of development
All economies rely only on services
Primary activities do not involve nature
solution: The chapter's overall message is that PRIMARY ACTIVITIES are the economic activities that EXTRACT and PRODUCE goods DIRECTLY from NATURE — from the Earth's natural resources — and form the FIRST, most BASIC stage of economic production (supplying food and raw materials that other sectors then process). The chapter surveys the main primary activities: HUNTING and GATHERING (the oldest and most primitive, depending directly on wild plants and animals); PASTORALISM (animal rearing) in two forms — NOMADIC HERDING (subsistence, in harsh arid/cold regions) and COMMERCIAL LIVESTOCK REARING/RANCHING (for the market); AGRICULTURE in its many forms — from PRIMITIVE SUBSISTENCE farming (including SHIFTING/slash-and-burn cultivation) and INTENSIVE SUBSISTENCE agriculture (small plots farmed intensively, especially rice, in densely populated monsoon Asia) to COMMERCIAL agriculture (commercial grain farming, MIXED farming, PLANTATION agriculture growing single cash crops like tea/coffee/rubber for export, and MARKET GARDENING/horticulture for urban markets); FISHING (a major source of food/protein, richest over cool continental shelves); FORESTRY/lumbering; and MINING (extracting minerals, by surface/open-cast or underground/shaft methods). These activities vary with the NATURAL ENVIRONMENT, TECHNOLOGY, and LEVEL of DEVELOPMENT, and they are MORE IMPORTANT (as a share of employment) in DEVELOPING countries — which rely heavily on agriculture — than in DEVELOPED countries, whose economies have shifted toward industry and services. So the overall message is option 2.
